Below it the body is split into two columns by a thin vertical divider at about 50% width: left column 'Regulators Mandating Privacy Rules / Policies' with two document images (EU GDPR and California State), right column 'Businesses Improving Privacy Management' with two phone screenshots (Facebook and Google), each column headed by centred bold labels with italic date lines. A thin grey rule runs above the footer at about 93% height; the source line is centred beneath it, the BOND logo sits bottom-left and the page number 167 sits bottom-right.

**Visuals**

Four images in a row, all boxed by thin dark grey frames with no crop. (1) EU GDPR: scanned white page of the Regulation (EU) 2016 text, centred bold serif heading 'REGULATION (EU) 2016/... OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL', body lines in small bold serif type, portrait orientation, black-and-white, no tint. (2) California State: scanned white page of Assembly Bill No. 375 Chapter 55, small justified serif text in two stacked sections, portrait, black-and-white. (3) Facebook: phone screenshot with blue status bar showing 2:04, header 'Privacy Shortcuts' with back arrow; flat illustration of three people on a teal band, text 'You're in control of privacy and security on Facebook.'; 'Privacy' section with grey outlined button 'MANAGE PRIVACY'; illustration of a building and person; 'Account Security' section with text 'Take actions to make your account more secure.' and outlined button 'MANAGE SECURITY'. (4) Google: phone screenshot on white with Google app icons row (Assistant, Maps, clock graphic with 'L', Google G) at top; heading 'Choose how long to keep your Web & App Activity'; three radio rows with calendar icons: 'Keep until I delete manually' (selected, filled blue radio), 'Keep for 18 months then delete automatically', 'Keep for 3 months then delete automatically'; 'How long is right for you?' followed by a paragraph; bottom buttons 'Cancel' in blue text and a solid blue 'Next' button. Also small BOND Internet Trends 2019 logo bottom-left, a grey page number 167 bottom-right.

**Text**

Can Amplify Polarization
Polarization has been abetted by many factors. Americans are sorting themselves out
geographically, living in increasingly politically homogeneous neighborhoods.
Social media & the proliferation of media channels via the Internet & TV has played
a role, allowing people to communicate exclusively with people like themselves.
Identity & the growth of identity politics have also played a role – People have gravitated
toward groups that feel they are in a zero-sum competition against one another.
Francis Fukuyama – Stanford University, Professor of Political Science, 12/18
Distribution of Democrats & Republicans
On 10-item Scale of Political Values, per Pew Research, USA
1994
2004
2017
MEDIAN Democrat MEDIAN Republican
Consistently liberal Consistently conservative
Pew Survey (USA)
BOND
Internet Trends
2019

### Slide 185

**Text**

We can definitely continue to improve how we manage the YouTube platform…
I see how much improvement we've already made…If you look back 2 years,
there were a lot of articles about how we handled violent extremism…
if you talk to experts in this field today, you can see we've made tremendous progress.
We are an information company - we committed last year to having >10,000 people moderating content…
I see how much progress we've already made. We just made changes to our
recommendation algorithms for borderline content & we've announced we've seen a
50% reduction in the views coming from recommendations on that content.
If you combine much better policies with technology to do that at scale,
I think you can be at a much better place.
Susan Wojcicki – CEO, YouTube, Interview @ Code Conference, 6/19
The Department of Homeland Security has engaged with major
social media companies to encourage them to continue to police their websites…
We do see that those efforts are bearing some fruit –
I think we have a long way to go & we look forward to continue
to engage with social media companies in that environment.
Brian Murphy – Principal Deputy Undersecretary, Department of Homeland Security, Testimony to USA Congress, 5/19

### Slide 189

**Text**

In a sense, the World Wide Web as we know it is over…
in its place is something altogether different:
a Balkanized ‘splinternet’…where your experience
online is determined by local regulation.
Mark Scott – Chief Technology Correspondent, Politico, 12/17 & 2/18
We need a new generation of laws
to govern a new generation of tech.
Brad Smith – President & Chief Legal Officer, Microsoft, 2/18
There’s a paradigm shift going on…
Governments are moving from a position of
non-interference to a realization that
if we want to keep a cross-border Internet going,
then we [need] a new system of governance.
Paul Fehlinger – Co-Founder, Internet & Jurisdiction Policy Network, 2/18
188
Internet Trends
2019
Note: ‘Splinternet’ originated by Clyde Wayne Crews Jr. writing for the Cato Institute in 2001.

**Layout**

Single centred column of three quotation blocks stacked top to bottom, each followed by a centred attribution line, separated by two thin full-width horizontal grey rules. A full-width navy band runs across the top 12.5% of the slide with no title text in it. The footer carries a centred grey note at the bottom, a small BOND wordmark and two-line Internet Trends 2019 label at bottom left, and the page number 188 at bottom right; a thin full-width light rule sits above the footer.

**Visuals**

Two horizontal rules in light grey (about #BFBFBF, roughly 0.1% of slide height thick) spanning about 4.1% to 94.2% of slide width, at about 41.3% and 59.6% of slide height. A navy header band (#00517A) across the top. A small grey BOND wordmark logo (60 by 15 pixels) at bottom left above the Internet Trends 2019 label. No photographs, charts or diagrams.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. White background with a full-width navy band (#00517A) across the top 12.5% of the slide. Quotation text is dark slate #2A3137 in Arial bold italic for the first and second quotes and Arial italic (regular weight) for the third quote, set at about 3.33% of slide height, centred. Attributions are Arial 2.04% of slide height, with the name in bold and the remainder in regular weight, same #2A3137. No shadows, gradients or corner radii.

### Slide 191

**Text**

Global Internet Freedom Framework (Freedom House)
Freedom House Freedom on The Net Index
Measures a country’s level of Internet / digital media freedom, using questions
derived from Article 19 of UN’s Universal Declaration of Human Rights:
Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion & expression; this right
includes freedom to hold opinions without interference & to seek, receive &
impart information & ideas through any media regardless of frontiers.
Countries are given points for: 1) Obstacles to Access; 2) Limits on Content; 3) Violations of User Rights
Free
Countries with low economic / infrastructural / regulatory barriers to Internet access…
minimal blocking / filtering of content / information…strong privacy protections
Partly-Free
Countries with some barriers to Internet access (like state-owned providers handicapping competition)…
some blocking of content / information (like news sites or temporary blocks on social media)…
some privacy violations (like data collection requirements with weak judicial oversight)
Not-Free
Countries with strong barriers to Internet access (like cutting off the internet to certain regions)
…strong blocking of content (news sites, opposition figures, permanent blocks on social media)…
rampant privacy violations (like data localization requirements with low judicial independence, unchecked surveillance)
BOND
Internet Trends
2019
Source: Freedom House’s Freedom on The Net Reports 2016-2018. Note: Freedom on the Net is a collaborative effort between a small team of Freedom House staff & an
extensive network of local researchers & advisors in 65 countries. Freedom on the Net’s in-country researchers have diverse backgrounds—academia, blogging, traditional
journalism, & tech— & track developments from their country of expertise. In the most repressive environments, Freedom House takes care to ensure researchers’
anonymity or, in exceptional cases, works with foreign nationals living outside their home country.

**Layout**

A full-width dark blue title band across the top holds a two-line left-aligned title with about 2% left margin. Below it, a centred double-headed arrow labelled Internet Regulation with Low at left and High at right sits above a grid of four centred-header columns (USA, 7 Largest EU Economies*, India, China) and a left row-label column with three rows (Internet Access, Content Regulation, User Regulation) separated by light grey rules. A centred legend box sits below the grid, and a footer with the BOND logo, Internet Trends 2019 wordmark, a centred grey note and the page number 191 at right sits along the bottom.

**Visuals**

A matrix diagram rather than a chart. Columns: USA (Global Internet User 8%), 7 Largest EU Economies* (8%*), India (12%), China (21%). Rows: Internet Access, Content Regulation, User Regulation. Each cell holds bulleted policy statements coloured by regulation level. USA: Internet Access green: 'Diverse regulatory bodies with varied distinct powers'; 'Privately-owned telecom infrastructure accessible to nearly all residents'. Content Regulation green: 'Virtually no content filtering & strong free speech protections'; 'No political censorship, strong protection for hosts of user-generated content'. User Regulation green: 'Some legal privacy protections related to government collection of user data'; 'Limited regulation on encryption / secure communication'. 7 Largest EU Economies: Internet Access green: same two statements as USA. Content Regulation yellow: 'Limited content filtering & free speech protections'; 'Limited political censorship, some liability for hosts of user-generated content'. User Regulation green: 'Strong legal privacy protections related to any collection of user data'; 'Limited regulation on encryption / secure communication'. India: Internet Access yellow: 'Diverse regulatory bodies, many with power to regulate access'; 'Government initiative to increase Internet access & usage as a public good'. Content Regulation yellow: 'Event-driven content filtering often without direct public input with some speech protection'; 'Some censorship, generally to remove insulting content'. User Regulation yellow: 'Some legal privacy protections related to government collection of user data'; 'Required government approval for encryption / secure communication'. China: Internet Access yellow: 'Central government bodies with strong regulatory power'; 'High government ownership / control of network infrastructure with ability to regulate access'. Content Regulation red: 'Strong content regulation & no expectation of speech protection'; 'Regulation to create a more harmonious digital society'. User Regulation red: 'Ability to collect user data for regulatory purposes'; 'Required government approval for encryption / secure communication'. Legend box: title Legend, then three coloured labels Limited Regulation (green), Moderate Regulation (yellow), Strong Regulation (red). No photographs, icons or illustrations; the only logo is the small BOND wordmark in the footer. Grid rules are thin light grey lines.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. Clean corporate white slide with a dark teal-blue title band. Title text is white regular Arial at about 4.4% of slide height. Column headers and row labels are bold grey Arial at about 2.6%. Policy cell text is regular Arial at about 1.5%, coloured green, amber or red by regulation level. Axis labels Low, High and Internet Regulation are bold charcoal Arial at about 3%. The legend box has a charcoal outline. Footer note is light grey Arial at about 1.2%, and the BOND wordmark and Internet Trends text are grey Georgia serif. Thin light grey rules, no shadows, no gradients, no rounded corners.

### Slide 193

**Text**

…World Wide Web =
Webs of Worlds Driven by Local Regulation
Global Internet Regulatory Observations per Foreign Affairs (9/18)
USA
European Union
In 1997, USA negotiated an agreement through the World Trade
Organization that committed 67 signatory countries to
‘procompetitive regulatory telecommunications principles’…
As the Internet grew more centralized & as its role expanded,
policymakers failed to keep up. When it came to updating
regulations for online activities…the Internet was treated as a
special realm that did not need regulation & the bad guys took notice.
Karen Kornbluh – Senior Fellow for Digital Policy, Council on Foreign Relations
The GDPR has…created a blueprint that other states &
organizations will study closely as they, too, seek to properly
balance individuals’ rights to data protection with their other
rights & with the legitimate interests of business & government.
The law’s main innovation is to establish a bedrock principle of
accountability. It places responsibility for properly collecting &
processing personal data squarely on organizations &
extends to individuals the right to prevent their data from
being collected or processed. The GDPR also gives
individuals the right to insist that their data be deleted.
Helen Dixon – Data Protection Commissioner, Ireland
India
China
When a service provider sends an authentication request to
Aadhaar (India’s National Identity System), the purpose of the
authentication is not revealed; all the government knows is when
someone uses his Aadhaar number, not where or why.
[Aadahaar shows] India’s approach to the Internet
is simple – empower users with the technical &
legal tools required to take back control of their data.
Nandan Nilekani – Founding Chair of Unique Identification Authority of India
Chinese leaders want to ensure a harmonious Internet – one that
guides public opinion, supports good governance & fosters
economic growth but also is tightly controlled…
China has promoted ‘cyber-sovereignty’ as an organizing
principle of Internet governance…China envisions
a world of national Internets, with government control
justified by the sovereign rights of states.
Adam Segal – Chair, Emerging Technologies & National Security, Council on Foreign Relations
BOND
Internet Trends
2019
Source: ’World War Web,’ Foreign Affairs, September / October Edition 2018
192

Footer: BOND logo and Internet Trends 2019 at bottom left, centred grey source line, slide number 192 at bottom right.

No charts, tables, photographs or diagrams.

### Slide 204

**Text**

First Step in Long Journey = / An Algorithmic Bill of Rights? / Crowdsourced Algorithmic Bill of Rights, per Sigal Samuel @ Vox / jack / @jack / Following / This is excellent. Great start. / Vox @voxdotcom / 1/ Many industries are increasingly leaning on algorithms to make decisions they say will be more efficient and impartial. But algorithms often end up reflecting human biases.... / Show this thread / 5:59 PM - 3 Jun 2019 / 10 things we should all demand from Big Tech right now / We need an algorithmic bill of rights. AI experts helped us write one. / By Sigal Samuel | Updated May 29, 2019, 9:00am EDT / The Highlight BY Vox / Transparency: We have the right to know when an algorithm is making a decision about us, which factors are being considered by the algorithm, and how those factors are being weighted. / Explanation: We have the right to be given explanations about how algorithms affect us in a specific situation, and these explanations should be clear enough that the average person will be able to understand them. / 1) Transparency / 2) Explanation / 3) Consent / 4) Freedom from Bias / 5) Feedback Mechanisms / 6) Data Portability / 7) Redress / 8) Algorithmic Literacy / 9) Independent Oversight / 10) Federal / Global Governance / BOND / Internet Trends / 2019 / Source: In early 2019, Vox reached out to 10 experts (including Kartik Hosanagar – original proposer of an Algorithmic Bill of Rights) at the forefront of investigating how Artificial Intelligence risk is creeping into multiple aspects of life. Vox reporter Sigal Samuel asked them each to name a protection the public needs enshrined in law, resulting in a crowdsourced, proposed Algorithmic Bill of Rights. Full detail available - https://www.vox.com/the-highlight/2019/5/22/18273284/ai-algorithmic-bill-of-rights-accountability-transparency-consent-bias / 203

### Slide 206

**Text**

A fundamental First Amendment principle is that all persons have access to places
where they can speak & listen & then, after reflection, speak & listen once more.
Today, one of the most important places to exchange views is cyberspace, particularly social
media, which offers relatively unlimited, low-cost capacity for communication of all kinds.
Anthony Kennedy – Former USA Supreme Court Justice – Majority Opinion, Packingham v. North Carolina, 6/2017
If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood & fallacies,
to avert the evil by the processes of education,
the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence.
Louis Brandeis – Former USA Supreme Court Justice – Concurring Opinion, Whitney v. California, 5/1927
I urge improving the governance capacity in cyberspace & developing
a governing network led by the [Communist Party of China].
Internet media should spread positive information, uphold the correct
political direction & guide public opinion & values towards the right direction.
Internet service providers should take responsibility to prevent cyberspace
from degrading into a platform full of harmful, false & provocative information.
Xi Jinping – President of The People’s Republic of China, As Translated by Xinhua, 4/2018
BOND
Internet Trends
2019
Source: USA Supreme Court (6/17). As translated to English by official China State media (Xinhua, 4/18)

Source: Identity Theft Resource Center (2014-2018). MalwareBytes 2019 State of Malware Report. Note: Trojan malware = malware specifically designed to evade detection by security software. Observed volume calculated as an average of monthly observations for a quarter. A sensitive record defined as personal information that could be used to commit a crime against a victim exposed due to an online security breach (e.g., bank credentials being accessed illicitly). Variation in number of records often driven by large individual breaches. In 2015, Anthem Health revealed 78MM personal records via breach. In 2017 Equifax exposed ~150MM personal records via breach. In 2018, Marriott International exposed ~383MM records via breach.

Effects Amplified by State Sponsorship

**Layout**

Full-width dark blue title band across the top 12.5% of the slide with a white two-line title left-aligned at about 1.9% from the left edge. Below it a centred bold italic question and a centred italic source credit, then three equal-width columns of ranked tables (February 2017, March 2018, March 2019) sitting side by side with headings centred above each; the table rows fill about 40% to 88% of the height. A thin light grey rule spans the full width at about 93% height, with the BOND logo and Internet Trends 2019 wordmark at lower left, the source note centred at the bottom, and the page number 217 at lower right (about 95.8% from left, 95.3% from top).

**Visuals**

Chart type: none. Three ranked text tables, one per survey wave, each with three columns: Rank (numerals, right-aligned), Concern (left-aligned labels), Share (percentages or numbers, right-aligned). February 2017 table rows: 1 Healthcare 36%; 2 Crime & Violence 33; 3 Terrorism 31; 4 Unemployment & Jobs 24 (highlighted); 5 Financial/Political Corruption 22; 6 Immigration 21; 7 Moral Decline 20; 8 Poverty & Social Inequality 19; 9 Taxes 17; 10 Education 16; 11 Climate Change 13; 12 Extremism 12; 13 Environmental Threats 9; 14 Maintaining Social Programs 7; 15 Inflation 6; 16 Childhood Obesity 3; 17 Access To Credit 2. **Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. Clean corporate report look. White background (#FFFFFF) with a dark teal-blue title band (#00517A). Title text is white regular sans-serif (Arial/Helvetica), about 4.4% of slide height per line, so roughly 9% of height for the two lines. Question text is bold italic sans-serif in dark slate #2A3137 at about 3.3% of slide height. Column headings are bold sans-serif #2A3137 at about 3.0%. Table body text is regular sans-serif at about 2.0%, in light grey #BFBFBF, with the Unemployment & Jobs rows in bold #C00000 red. Table header rules are heavy dark slate #2A3137 (about 0.2% of height thick); row separators are thin light grey lines. Source line and footer text are light grey sans-serif around 1.3%. Internet Trends and 2019 are in a grey serif (Georgia) #C8C8C8. Page number is grey #A6A6A6 sans-serif. No shadows, gradients, rounded corners or boxes.

### Slide 219

**Text**

Consumer Confidence Index (USA) = High & Rising… / @ 97 vs. 88 Sixty-Five Year Average / Consumer Confidence Index (CCI) / 120 / 88 = / 65-Year Average / CCI (Indexed to 1966), USA / 60 / 0 / 1954 1959 1964 1969 1974 1979 1984 1989 1994 1999 2004 2009 2014 2019 / BOND / Internet Trends / 2019 / Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve FRED Database. Note: Indexed to Q1:66 = 100. Consumer Confidence Index (Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index) is a / broad measure of American consumer sentiment, as measured through a 50-question telephone survey of at least 500 USA residents each month. / 218

**Layout**

A full-width navy title band spans the top 12.5% of the slide with a two-line left-aligned title starting at x 2.1%, y 1.7%. Below it a single chart is centred in the white body, with its chart title centred above the plot; the footer rule sits at about 93% of the height, with the BOND logo and Internet Trends/2019 block at the bottom left, a centred two-line source note in the middle, and the page number 218 at bottom right.

**Visuals**

One line chart. Type: line chart, time series. Chart title: Consumer Confidence Index (CCI), bold dark grey, centred above plot. Y-axis: title 'CCI (Indexed to 1966), USA'; ticks 0, 60, 120 (range 0 to 120, linear, unitless index). X-axis: years 1954 to 2019, ticks every 5 years (1954, 1959 ... 2019), no axis title. Series: one monthly Consumer Confidence Index line, dark navy #00517A, about 2.5 pt stroke, no markers. Values are not printed; estimates: about 107 in 1964, about 54 at the 1979 trough, about 110 at the 1999 peak, about 97 at the latest point (2019). Reference series: a dashed horizontal line in crimson #C82055 at 88 labelled '88 = 65-Year Average' (bold 88) placed under the 1954 to 1966 section of the line. Legend: none. Highlighted points: none beyond the crimson 88 reference line. Gridlines: light grey horizontal lines at 120, 60 and 0. No photograph, icon or logo other than the BOND wordmark.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF covering the whole slide. White slide background with a navy #00517A header band across the top 12.5%. Title and subtitle are white regular Arial (ArialMT) sans-serif, about 4.4% of slide height, set flush left in two lines. Chart title is bold Arial (Arial-BoldMT) dark slate #3C444C, about 4.4% of slide height. Chart axis labels and axis title are light grey #BFBFBF Arial about 2.2% of height. Reference label and dashed line are crimson #C82055 Arial, about 2.6% of height, with '88' in bold. Source note is light grey #BFBFBF Arial about 1.3% of height. Page number is grey #A6A6A6 Arial about 1.5%. Brand text 'Internet Trends' and '2019' are light grey #C8C8C8 Georgia serif about 1.5%. Shapes are flat with no shadows, rounded corners or gradients.

Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve FRED Database, Bureau of Economic Analysis, BLS. Note: Real GDP based on chained 2012 dollars. Unemployment rate = annual average. *A job opening
is defined as a non-farm specific position of employment to be filled at an establishment. Conditions include the following: there is work available for that position, the job could start within 30

**Layout**

Full-width dark blue title band across the top with a two-line white title left-aligned at a small left margin. Below it sits a three-column row of charts (two-thirds-wide left chart, narrow middle chart, right chart) separated by two thin vertical grey rules, each with a bold grey heading above it; the source footnote runs across the bottom with a BOND logo at lower left, 'Internet Trends 2019' beneath it, and the page number 219 at lower right.

**Visuals**

Three charts. Chart 1, titled Real GDP vs. Unemployment Rate, USA: line chart with two series on dual axes. Left axis Real GDP in trillions of dollars, $0 to $24T, gridlines at $12T and $24T, x-axis labels 1928, 1958, 1988, 2018. Right axis Unemployment Rate in percent, 0% to 30%, labels 0%, 15%, 30%. Red series Civilian Unemployment (#C00000), about 25% peak near 1932-33, about 2% to 3% around 1940s, about 6% near 1960s-70s, about 10% near 2010 and about 4% at 2018; Real GDP blue series (#00517A) starting about $0.6T in 1928, rising to about $18.5T at 2018, values estimated. Legend below left axis: red bar with Civilian Unemployment, blue bar with Real GDP. Chart 2, titled Job Openings, USA: filled area chart in grey #8A99A6, y-axis Job Openings* in millions (MM) from 0 to 10MM with gridline at 5MM, x-axis 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018. About 5.8MM at 2000, falling to about 2.2MM near 2009, rising to about 7.6MM at 2018; values estimated, none printed. Chart 3, titled Median Real Weekly Earnings, All Workers Over 16, USA: green line (#00B050) on y-axis Median Usual Weekly Wage from $320 to $360 with gridlines at $340 and $360, x-axis 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018. About $329 at 2000, about $329 low near 2006, about $345 around 2008-2009, about $350 near 2012 to 2014, about $355 at 2018; values estimated, none printed. Two thin grey vertical divider lines separate the charts. Footer BOND logo image, a small grey serif wordmark.

**Design**

Background: Plain white #FFFFFF. Clean corporate look on a white field. Title band #00517A (dark teal blue) with white title in regular sans-serif (Arial-like) at about 4.3% of slide height for the title text. Chart headings in bold Arial-like sans-serif #3C444C at about 2.2% of slide height, centered. Axis labels and footnote in light grey #BFBFBF sans-serif at about 1.5% (labels) and 1.3% (footnote). Series colours: #C00000 red, #00517A blue, #8A99A6 grey fill, #00B050 green. Gridlines light grey #D9D9D9 hairlines, about 1 px. Vertical divider rules mid grey #A6A6A6, about 1.5 px. No shadows, gradients, rounded corners or boxes. Logo and tagline in grey Georgia-like serif #C8C8C8.

**Layout**

Full-width dark blue title band across the top with two white title lines left-aligned at the left margin, then two bold italic section headers centred over a left column (Real-Time Platforms) and a right two-column area (Internet-Enabled Marketplaces), separated by a thin grey horizontal rule and a thin vertical grey divider. Below, a 2-column by 3-row grid of small chart panels: left column has Uber (top) and DoorDash (bottom); right area has Etsy, Airbnb (top row) and Wonolo, VIPKid (bottom row). Each panel has a centred bold title above its chart and a legend below. A thin grey footer rule sits near the bottom with a centred grey source note, BOND logo and 'Internet Trends 2019' lower left, and page number 227 lower right.

**Visuals**

Six combination and line charts, all with white background and light grey horizontal gridlines, no border. Axis labels and tick labels in light grey #BFBFBF; axis titles rotated vertically in light grey. Tick values are printed only on some axes.
1) Uber @ 4MM Driver-Partners: combo chart. Left axis Gross Bookings, Global, $0 to $60B (ticks $0, $30B, $60B). Right axis Driver-Partners, Global, 0 to 6MM (ticks 0, 3MM, 6MM). X categories 2014 to 2018. Series Gross Bookings as dark blue #00517A columns, about $3B (2014), about $9B (2015), about $19B (2016), about $34B (2017), about $49B (2018). Series Driver-Partners as dark maroon line #A81E4B, starting 2015 at about 1.1MM, rising to about 3.9MM in 2018, with markers absent. Legend below: blue bar Gross Bookings, maroon line Driver-Partners.
2) Etsy @ 2MM Sellers: combo chart. Left axis Gross Merchandise Sales (GMS), Global, $0 to $4B (ticks $0, $2B, $4B). Right axis Sellers, Global, 0 to 4MM (ticks 2MM, 4MM). X 2012 to 2018 in two-year ticks. GMS as dark blue #00517A columns, about $0.9B (2012), $1.3B (2013), $1.9B (2014), $2.4B (2015), $2.8B (2016), $3.2B (2017), $3.9B (2018). Sellers as maroon #A81E4B line, about 0.8MM (2012) rising to about 2.1MM (2018). Legend: GMS bar, Sellers line.
3) Airbnb @ 6MM Listings: combo chart. Left axis Guest Arrivals, Global, 0 to 250MM (ticks 0, 125MM, 250MM). Right axis Active Listings, Global, 0 to 6MM (ticks 0, 3MM, 6MM). X 2010 to 2018 in two-year ticks. Guest Arrivals dark blue #00517A columns, very small before 2014, about 16MM (2014), about 39MM (2015), about 79MM (2016), about 149MM (2017), about 200MM (2018). Active Listings bright pink-red #C8215A line, rising from near 0 in 2011 to about 5.8MM in 2018 with steepening slope. Legend: Guest Arrivals bar, Active Listings line.
4) DoorDash @ 1.3MM Dashers: line chart only, left axis Lifetime Dashers, Global, 0 to 1.4MM (ticks 0, 0.7MM, 1.4MM). X 2014 to 2019. Single pink-red #C8215A line, about 0 (2014), 0.03MM (2015), 0.08MM (2016), 0.2MM (2017), 0.72MM (2018), 1.31MM (2019). Legend: Lifetime Dashers line.
5) Wonolo @ 230K Workers: line chart, left axis Onboarded Workers, Global, 0 to 250K (ticks 0, 125K, 250K). X 2014 to 2018. Single pink-red #C8215A line, about 1K (2014), 9K (2015), 27K (2016), 90K (2017), 230K (2018). Legend: Onboarded Workers line.
6) VIPKid @ 70K Teachers: combo chart. Left axis Students, Global, 0 to 900K (ticks 0, 450K, 900K). Right axis Teachers, Global, 0 to 110K (ticks 0, 55K, 110K). X 2017 to 2019. Teachers as dark blue #00517A columns, about 250K (2017), about 490K (2018), about 575K (2019) on left axis. Students as red #C00000 line on right axis, about 25K (2017), about 37K (2018), about 74K (2019)... Legend: Teachers bar, Students line. No highlighted points. Note: the Students line is plotted on the 0 to 110K right scale as printed.
Logo: BOND wordmark in serif grey at lower left, a small image (about 60 by 15 pixels) at x 4.1 y 94.4.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF covering the whole slide, with a dark blue #00517A band across the top 12.5% of the height. Clean corporate chart slide. Background white #FFFFFF. Title band fill #00517A (deep teal blue). Title text white #FFFFFF, regular sans-serif (Arial-like), about 4.4% of slide height per line, left-aligned, two lines. Section headers bold italic sans-serif (Arial Bold Italic) in dark charcoal #2A3137, about 3.7% of slide height, centred. Chart titles bold sans-serif (Arial Bold) #2A3137 about 2.2% of height, centred over each panel. Axis and tick labels regular Arial in #BFBFBF about 1.5% of height; legend text regular Arial #2A3137 about 1.5%. Footer source text Arial #BFBFBF about 1.3% of height, centred. Page number Arial #A6A6A6 about 1.5%. BOND logo and 'Internet Trends' in Georgia-like serif, #C8C8C8. Lines: horizontal divider and footer rule thin light grey #BFBFBF about 1 px; vertical divider thin grey. Bars solid fill, no shadows, no gradients, square corners. Lines are about 3 px wide, no markers. No shadows or gradients anywhere.

Remote Workers =
Enabled by Online Collaboration Tools
Remote Workforce (Zapier)
Danny Schreiber 11:35 AM
@channel heads up -- publish dates in Trello are now set to 4 a.m. -- this makes is globally the same day for us all 😊
http://i.imgur.com/wt11vUS.png (12KB)
Due Date
Feb 17 at 4:00 AM
now no more confusion for our Bangkok office, hehe
Matthew Guay 11:37 AM
😊 Nice stuff, thanks for getting that figured out @danny!
time zones are more annoying than exchange rates
At Zapier, we’ve found that by using a stack of collaboration tools that work well together, our 100% remote team is able to work more efficiently, regardless of where they’re located.
It’s important for us to have the ability to instantly access a folder, collaborate on a shared document, or chat in real time.
With well-connected tools & processes, any remote employee can feel more focused, productive & in control of their time.
Wade Foster – Co-Founder / CEO, Zapier, 6/19
Highest-Use Apps on Zapier
Y/Y Growth
By Remote Teams
1/18-1/19
1) Slack +42%
2) Google Sheets +59%
3) Airtable +37%

Source: National Center for Education Statistics (3/18). 2017-2018 are estimates supplied by Chegg. *Note: Decline in Post-Secondary Students only taking offline courses partly driven by student
demographics (e.g., an older student base more likely to be employed while at school).  Data through 1995 are for institutions of higher education, while later data are for degree-granting institutions.
Degree-granting institutions grant associate’s or higher degrees & participate in Title IV federal financial aid programs. The degree-granting classification is very similar to the earlier higher education
classification, but it includes more 2-year colleges & excludes a few higher education institutions that did not grant degrees. Some data have been revised from previously published figures.

**Layout**

Single-slide layout with a full-width dark blue title band across the top, containing a two-line left-aligned white title starting about 1.9% from the left edge. Below the band the body is two columns split by a thin vertical divider at about 50% of slide width: a stacked area chart on the left (chart title centred above it) and a line chart on the right (chart title centred above it), with the axis caption and legend beneath. A thin grey rule and a footer row sit at the bottom with a BOND logo image and 'Internet Trends 2019' at left, a centred-left source note in four lines, and the page number 237 at the right edge.

**Visuals**

Chart 1 (left): stacked area chart titled 'Post-Secondary Education – Enrollments*'. Y axis 'Undergraduate Enrollments, USA' from 0 to 26MM with labelled ticks 0, 13MM, 26MM and horizontal gridlines at 0, 13MM and 26MM. X axis 1970 to 2018 with labelled ticks 1970, 1986, 2002, 2018. Three stacked series from bottom: 2 Year Undergraduate in dark blue #00517A (about 3MM in 1970 rising to about 7MM by 2010 and about 5.5MM in 2018), 4 Year Undergraduate in light grey #BFBFBF (the band between the blue and maroon top), and Any Graduate in maroon #640F2A (the top band, about 1.5MM to 3MM thick, peaking near 2010 at about 24MM total). Values are estimates marked about; the slide prints no values. Thin white outlines separate the bands. Legend below the chart: dark blue line swatch with '2 Year Undergraduate', grey line swatch with '4 Year Undergraduate', maroon line swatch with 'Any Graduate' on a second row. Chart 2 (right): line chart titled 'Post-Secondary Students – % in Only Offline Courses'. Y axis '% Students Taking Only Offline Courses, USA' from 0% to 100% with gridlines at 0%, 50% and 100%. X axis school years 2012 to 2017 labelled 'Year = School Year Beginning in Fall'. One green #14AB81 line about 2.5pt thick, falling from about 74% in 2012 to 67% in 2017 with labelled points 74% (above-left of the 2012 point) and 67% (below the 2017 point); intermediate points are about 2013 near 73%, 2014 near 72%, 2015 near 70%, 2016 near 68%, all estimates. Vertical grey divider line between the two charts. Footer: BOND wordmark logo image, small Georgia text 'Internet Trends' and '2019'.

**Layout**

A full-width dark blue title band occupies the top 12.5% of the slide, with a two-line white title left-aligned at about 1.9% from the left edge. A bold centred subtitle sits below the band, followed by a grey right-pointing arrow spanning the width with four green year labels (2016, 2017, 2018, 2019) centred on the columns. Institution boxes are arranged in four columns: one box under 2016, two stacked under 2017, one under 2018, and seven stacked under 2019; the 2019 column extends down to about 90.7%. A thin grey rule sits at about 93% height; the source line is centred beneath it, the BOND Internet Trends 2019 logo is bottom-left and the page number 240 is bottom-right.

**Visuals**

Timeline diagram with no photographs, charts or icons. A light grey (#D9D9D9) block arrow runs horizontally at about 22% to 30% of slide height across x 5.2% to 94.8%, with its triangular head pointing right at the far end above the 2019 column. The four year labels sit on the arrow body in bold green. Below each year, white rectangles with thin light-grey (#BFBFBF) outlines hold an institution name in bold dark text and one or two degree names in italic light grey. The boxes are not connected by lines; they are arranged by year and stacked vertically in the 2019 column. The 2016 column has one box, 2017 has two (HEC Paris above University of Illinois), 2018 has one (Arizona State University), and 2019 has seven: University of Pennsylvania, University of London, Macquarie University, University of Michigan, Imperial College London, University of Colorado Boulder. A small BOND logo image (60 by 15 px, grey serif wordmark) sits bottom-left.

**Design**

**Layout**

Full-width navy title band across the top 12.5% of the slide with a two-line left-aligned title starting at about 1.9% from the left edge. Below it, a centred bold subtitle sits at about 17.5% height above a single wide financial table spanning roughly 4.9% to 95.8% of the width, with a seven-column numeric block (F1988 to F2018) followed by a Comments column separated by a gap. Footer: BOND logo bottom-left, Georgia 'Internet Trends' and '2019' beneath it, a centred three-line grey source note bottom-centre, and page number 264 bottom-right.

### Slide 268

**Text**

…USA Entitlements = / 61% vs. 42% of Government Spending Thirty Years Ago / USA Expenses by Category / $1.1T / $4.1T / 1988 / → / 2018 / 1988 → 2018 / Change / 8% / 14% / 100% / 10% / 16% / 16% / Debt* / +$14T (+668%) / 15% / Entitlements / +$2.1T (+463%) / 27% / 61% / Non-Defense / Discretionary / +$465B (+268%) / USA 10Y Treasury Yield / 50% / 5% / Defense / USA Expenses / +$332B (+114%) / 42% / Net Interest Cost: / +$173B (+114%) / 1988 / 2018 / 0% / 0% / Entitlements / Mandatory / Defense / 10 Year Treasury Yield / Non-Defense Discretionary / Net Interest Cost / 267 / BOND / Internet Trends / 2019 / Source: Congressional Budget Office, White House Office of Management & Budget, USA Treasury / *Debt reflects net debt (i.e. excludes debt issued by The Treasury & owned by other Government accounts) / Note: Yellow line represents yield on 10-year USA Treasury bill from 12/31/87 to 12/31/18.

**Layout**

Single full-width chart slide with a dark blue title band across the top spanning the full width, the title left-aligned at the top-left margin in two lines. Below the band, a chart title is centred over the stacked-column chart on the left about two-thirds of the width, with a boxed change panel on the right; a legend sits below the chart, and a thin footer rule with the BOND logo at bottom-left, source notes centred and page number 267 at bottom-right closes the slide.

**Visuals**

Chart: stacked 100% column chart titled USA Expenses by Category, with two columns for 1988 (total labelled $1.1T) and 2018 (total labelled $4.1T). Left axis USA Expenses 0% to 100% in 50% steps, labelled in grey; right axis USA 10Y Treasury Yield 0% to 10% in 5% steps. Stacks from bottom to top in 1988: Entitlements / Mandatory 42%, Defense 27%, Non-Defense Discretionary 16%, Net Interest Cost 14%. In 2018: Entitlements / Mandatory 61%, Defense 15%, Non-Defense Discretionary 16%, Net Interest Cost 8%. Series 10 Year Treasury Yield is a yellow line with no printed values, plotted against the right axis, starting near about 6.5% in 1988 region, falling to about 1% to 3% by 2018 with fluctuations; about values are estimates. A thin dark blue connector line runs from top of 1988 Entitlements segment to top of 2018 Entitlements segment and a thin dark blue baseline runs along 0% between the columns. Legend below chart in two rows: square markers with Entitlements / Mandatory (blue), Defense (grey), Non-Defense Discretionary (green), Net Interest Cost (maroon) and a short yellow line for 10 Year Treasury Yield. Right panel: white box with dark grey border containing 1988 to 2018 Change heading and four figures with a red bracket with arrowheads linking Debt* to Net Interest Cost. No photographs, logos other than the BOND wordmark.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. White background with a dark blue title band #00517A across the top 12.5 percent of slide height. Title text white ArialMT regular, about 4.4 percent of slide height, two lines. Chart title and column totals in bold dark grey Arial #3C444C at about 3.7 percent (chart title) and 2.6 percent (totals). Body and axis text Arial regular in grey #BFBFBF for axes and dark grey #3C444C for legend. Segment labels bold white Arial about 2.2 percent. Colours: Entitlements #00517A, Defense #BFBFBF, Non-Defense Discretionary #18573B, Net Interest Cost #640F2A, 10 year yield line yellow #FFC000 approximately. Panel box has thin dark grey border and no fill (white). Connector and bracket lines thin, dark blue and crimson red #C0173D approximately with small triangular arrowheads. No corner radii, shadows or gradients. Footer rule light grey. Footer source text Arial about 1.3 percent, grey #BFBFBF. Logo wordmark BOND in Georgia serif grey, Internet Trends Georgia light grey #C8C8C8.

**Layout**

Two equal chart panels sit side by side below a full-width dark blue title band, separated by a thin vertical grey divider at about x 50%. The title is left-aligned in the band at the top left with a margin of about 2% of the width, and the chart headings are centred over each panel. The source footnote is centred under a thin light grey horizontal rule near the bottom, the BOND logo and Internet Trends wordmark sit at bottom left, and the page number 270 sits at bottom right.

**Visuals**

Two charts. Left: a line chart titled Health Expenditures – % of Government Total, USA. Y axis is titled Health Expenditure (% of Total Expenditure) with tick labels 0%, 15% and 30% (about 0 to 30 percent, gridlines at 15% and 30%). X axis has tick labels 1987, 1992, 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, annual data from 1987 to 2017. Three series: Total USA Government (dark blue #00517A) rises from about 10% in 1987 to about 23.5% in 2017, with a dip around 2008 to 2009; Federal Government (green #00B050) rises from about 5.4% in 1987 to about 14.6% in 2017, with a small dip near 2009; State / Local Government (red #C00000) rises from about 4.9% in 1987 to about 8.9% in 2017, with a dip near 2009 to about 7%. No values are printed on the lines; all values are estimates marked about. Legend below the chart: Total USA Government (dark blue swatch) on the first row; Federal Government (green swatch) and State / Local Government (red swatch) on the second row. Right: a horizontal stacked bar chart titled Health Expenditures – % of GDP, 2017, per OECD. Y axis titled Health Spend (% of GDP) lists 26 countries from top to bottom. X axis 0%, 10%, 20% with light grey vertical gridlines at 10% and 20%. Each bar stacks Government / Compulsory (light grey #BFBFBF, first segment) and Voluntary (dark blue #00517A, second segment); the USA bar is outlined by a thin red #C00000 rectangle and its label is in red bold. Estimated values (about, read from the bars, no values printed): USA grey about 14.1%, total about 17.2%; Switzerland grey about 7.7%, total about 12.2%; France about 9.5% and 11.5%; Germany about 9.6% and 11.3%; Sweden about 9.1% and 10.9%; Japan about 9.0% and 10.7%; Canada about 7.3% and 10.4%; Austria about 7.7% and 10.3%; The Netherlands about 8.3% and 10.2%; Belgium about 8.0% and 10.0%; Great Britain about 7.7% and 9.6%; Finland about 6.9% and 9.2%; Australia about 6.3% and 9.1%; New Zealand about 7.2% and 8.9%; Italy about 6.7% and 8.8%; Spain about 6.3% and 8.8%; Greece about 5.2% and 8.3%; Chile about 5.0% and 8.1%; Korea about 4.4% and 7.6%; Israel about 4.7% and 7.4%; Hungary about 4.9% and 7.2%; Ireland about 5.2% and 7.0%; Czech Republic about 5.8% and 7.0%; Poland about 4.6% and 6.7%; Mexico about 2.8% and 5.4%; Turkey about 3.3% and 4.2%. Legend at bottom right: Government / Compulsory (grey swatch) and Voluntary (dark blue swatch). Bars are thick, about 75% of row pitch, with no outlines except the USA highlight. Small BOND logo at bottom left: a grey serif wordmark reading BOND in capitals, boxed by nothing.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF background. Clean corporate report style on white. Title band is solid dark blue #00517A across the top 12.5% of the height with white #FFFFFF title text in a regular sans-serif (Arial-like) at about 4.4% of slide height, two lines. Chart headings are bold sans-serif (Arial Bold) in charcoal #2A3137 at about 3.0% of slide height. Axis labels, tick labels and country labels are regular Arial in light grey #BFBFBF at about 1.1% to 1.8% of slide height. Series colours: dark blue #00517A, green #00B050, red #C00000. Legend text colours: #2A3137 for Total USA Government, #00283D for Federal Government, #320815 for State / Local Government, #BFBFBF for Government / Compulsory, #00517A for Voluntary. Footnote is light grey #BFBFBF Arial at about 1.3%. Footer wordmarks use Georgia serif in pale grey #C8C8C8; page number is Arial in #A6A6A6. Lines are thin: 1 to 2 px grey vertical divider #BFBFBF and horizontal rule #D9D9D9. No shadows, no gradients, no rounded corners.

**Layout**

Two-column layout below a full-width dark blue title band; a left panel holds a horizontal bar chart and a right panel holds a line chart, separated by a thin vertical grey divider at about 50% of slide width. Title is left-aligned in white at top-left inside the band with about 1.9% left margin. Column headings are bold, centred over each panel. A footer rule sits near the bottom, with the BOND logo and Internet Trends 2019 at bottom left, centred source note in the middle, and page number 276 at bottom right.

**Visuals**

Left: horizontal bar chart, untitled axes, chart heading 'Top Physician ‘Wants’ for Future EHR Development, per Stanford / Harris Poll, 9/18'. Three bars in #00517A, category labels to the left in bold: Interoperability 67%, Predictive Analytics 43%, Financial / Cost Data Integration 32%. Value labels bold dark grey right of each bar. Horizontal value axis 0% to 80% labelled at 0%, 40%, 80% in light grey, with light grey vertical gridlines at those values. No legend, no highlighted points. Right: line chart titled 'EHR Adoption, USA'. Y-axis '% Using E.H.R. System' rotated, labelled 0%, 50%, 100%, light grey horizontal gridlines at each. X-axis years 2004 to 2016, labels at 2-year intervals. Series Hospitals (#00517A dark blue line, about 2011 to 2016): about 72% in 2011, about 85% in 2012, about 94% in 2013, about 97% in 2014, about 96% in 2015, about 96% in 2016. Series Physician’s Offices (#00B050 green line, 2004 to 2015): about 21% in 2004, about 24% in 2005, about 30% in 2006, about 35% in 2007, about 42% in 2008, about 48% in 2009, about 51% in 2010, about 57% in 2011, about 72% in 2012, about 79% in 2013, about 83% in 2014, about 87% in 2015. Legend below chart: dark blue line segment labelled Hospitals, green line segment labelled Physician’s Offices. Lines are about 0.5% of slide height thick with no markers. Small BOND logo image at bottom left, 60 by 15 pixels.

**Text**

Online Discovery = Improving Accessibility + Availability of Care Optimizing Perishable Inventory = Accelerating Access to Care Zocdoc = Digital Healthcare Marketplace Zocdoc Monthly Patients, USA 8MM 4MM 0 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 Zocdoc Monthly Patients, USA Healthcare providers partner with Zocdoc to fill their 20-30% unused, perishable inventory. This dramatically accelerates access to care for patients. While patients who call wait an average of 24 days to get in to see a doctor, when booking online via Zocdoc, the typical appointment happens within 24-72 hours. Because of this win/win, in our first market NYC, one in five new patient-doctor relationships is established via Zocdoc. Our other markets are following the same trajectory. Clover Health (3/19). Note: Enrollment includes cost plans & Medicare Advantage Plans. Approximately 61MM people are enrolled in Medicare in 2018.

**Layout**

Two equal side-by-side chart panels divided by a thin vertical grey rule at the slide centre, under a full-width dark blue title band across the top. Each panel has a bold centred two-line heading above a light grey centred chart subtitle, then a line chart with its own vertical axis title on the left and year labels along the bottom. The title is left-aligned in the band with a left margin of about 2 percent. The footer has a BOND logo and Internet Trends 2019 text at bottom left, a centred three-line source note, and the page number 285 at bottom right, separated from the body by a thin light grey rule.

**Visuals**

Two line charts, both with no legend and no highlighted points. Left chart: Medicare Advantage Enrollment, USA. Y axis titled Medicare Advantage Enrollment, USA, range 0 to 22MM, labelled gridlines at 0, 11MM and 22MM. X axis labelled 1999, 2004, 2009, 2014, 2018. Single green series (#00B050, about 3pt stroke) with values estimated, as none are printed: about 6.9MM in 1999, falling to about 5.3MM around 2003-2004, rising steadily to about 20.4MM in 2018. Right chart: Clover Health Members, USA. Y axis titled Medicare Advantage Members, USA, range 0 to 40K, labelled gridlines at 0, 20K and 40K. X axis labelled 2015 to 2019 at yearly intervals. Single navy series (#00517A, about 3pt stroke) with estimated values: about 7.1K in 2015, about 16.7K in 2016, about 20K in 2016.5, about 25K in 2017.5, about 32K in 2018.8 and about 40K at 2019; no values printed. Gridlines are light grey (#D9D9D9, about 1pt). A thin grey vertical rule (#808080) divides the two panels. Footer BOND logo is a small image of the word BOND in grey serif capitals, 60 by 15 pixels.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF covering the whole slide, with a #00517A band across the top 12.5 percent. Clean corporate report style with white background. Title band is solid #00517A with white title text in Arial regular, about 4.4 percent of slide height per line. Chart headings are Arial bold in near-black #2A3137 at about 3.0 percent of slide height. Chart subtitles are Arial bold in light grey #BFBFBF at about 1.8 percent. Axis labels and year labels are Arial regular #BFBFBF at about 1.8 percent. Body text is Arial in grey and navy. Footer source note is Arial regular #BFBFBF at about 1.3 percent. Footer brand text Internet Trends and 2019 is Georgia serif in #C8C8C8 at about 1.5 percent. Page number is Arial regular #A6A6A6 at about 1.5 percent. Lines are thin and square-ended; there are no shapes with rounded corners, shadows or gradients.

291

**Layout**

A full-width dark blue title band runs across the top 12.5% of the slide with a two-line white title left-aligned at about 1.9% from the left edge. Below it the body is split into two columns by a thin vertical grey divider at 50% of the slide width: the left column (PillPack) is centred on about x=25% with two phone screenshots, an italic quote and an attribution; the right column holds a horizontal bar chart with headings centred on about x=75%. A thin grey rule spans the width at about 93% of the slide height, below which a centred source note sits, the BOND logo and 'Internet Trends 2019' lie bottom-left, and the page number 291 sits bottom-right.

**Visuals**

Two phone screenshots side by side in the left column, then a horizontal bar chart in the right column. Left screenshot (medications list): white phone-style screen with a charcoal (#2A3137) border, bold black heading 'Medications', a blue (#00517A-like, #1F9BD7) '+ Add a Prescription' row, then four rows with a small pill icon, bold uppercase name and '8:00 AM' beneath: LISINOPRIL 5 MG, METOPROLOL 25 MG, OMEPRAZOLE 10 MG, SIMVASTATIN 5 MG, each with a chevron at right; a divider, then 'As Needed' bold heading and a row 'PROAIR HFA INHALER' with an inhaler icon. Right screenshot (messages): white phone screen with charcoal border, header 'Call' at left, 'Messages' centred, 'Done' at right in blue; light blue (#3CB4F0) outgoing bubbles with white text: 'Hi! [smiley emoji] Can I move all my medications to 8am and 8pm?', 'Actually, yeah. Could I get my multivitamin in a bottle instead of my PillPack?', 'Thanks!' with 'Delivered' beneath; light grey (#E5E5E5) incoming bubbles with dark text: 'No problem! I've updated your medication schedule. Is there anything else I can help you with?' and 'Sure thing. We'll ship your multivitamin in a separate bottle with your next PillPack.'; a small circular head-and-shoulders photo of a man beside 'Emily H.' and 'New Hampshire'; a grey sender label 'Emily H.' under the last grey bubble. Chart: horizontal bar chart titled 'Prescription Medicine Usage, 2019, USA' (light grey bold); x-axis 0% to 60% with tick labels 0%, 30%, 60% and axis title '% of Respondents, USA'; vertical light grey gridlines at 0%, 30% and 60%. Three bars: '1-3 prescription drugs' about 37% (dark blue #00517A), '>4 prescription drugs' 24% (dark blue #00517A), 'Do not take prescription medicine' 38% (light grey #BFBFBF). Values printed at bar ends: 37%, 24%, 38%. A dark blue square bracket at the left of the first two bars groups them, labelled '62% Take Prescription Drugs' (62% in bold). No legend; no highlighted points beyond the colour difference between the blue and grey bars. Logo: BOND wordmark at bottom-left.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. Clean corporate look on a white background. Title band fill #00517A with white regular title text. Headings bold #2A3137 charcoal. Body and quote italic #4A4A4A. Chart labels #2A3137 with grey #BFBFBF for the non-taking category, axis labels and chart title. Accent colour #00517A for bars, bracket, and title band. Typeface: Arial (ArialMT / Arial-BoldMT / Arial-ItalicMT), sans-serif. Title about 4.44% of slide height, headings about 2.96%, body about 1.84%, quote about 2.6%, source note about 1.29%. Lines: thin light grey divider (about 1px #BFBFBF); bracket stroke about 3px #00517A; gridlines about 1px light grey. Bars are flat rectangles with square corners. No shadows or gradients. Screenshots have square charcoal borders.

**Layout**

Two equal-width chart panels side by side below a full-width dark blue title band, separated by a thin vertical grey divider at about 50% of slide width. Title is left-aligned in the band starting at about 2% from the left edge, with the two-line title occupying the top 12.5%. Chart headings are centred above each panel; legends sit below the charts, and a grey rule and three-line source note run across the bottom with the BOND logotype and Internet Trends 2019 credit at lower left and the page number 292 at lower right.

**Visuals**

Two charts. (1) Left: line chart titled Health Expenditures % of Government Total, USA. Y axis titled Health Expenditure (% of Total Expenditure), range 0% to 30% with gridlines at 0%, 15% and 30%. X axis years 1987 to 2017 labelled every five years (1987, 1992, 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017). Three series: Total USA Government (dark blue #00517A line, about 10.2% in 1987 rising to about 17% in 2000, dipping near 2009, about 23.5% in 2017); Federal Government (green #00B050 line, about 5.4% in 1987, about 9% in 2000, about 12.5% in 2010, about 14.7% in 2017); State / Local Government (red #C00000 line, about 4.9% in 1987, about 6.5% in 2000, about 6.8% in 2008 with a dip to about 5.6% around 2009, about 8.9% in 2017). All values are estimates read from the chart, which prints no values. Legend: Total USA Government on its own row above; Federal Government and State / Local Government on a row below. Lines are about 3 px wide, no markers. (2) Right: horizontal stacked bar chart titled Health Expenditures, % of GDP, 2017, per OECD. Value axis 0% to 20% with gridlines at 0%, 10% and 20%; category axis Health Spend (% of GDP) listing 25 countries from top to bottom: USA, Switzerland, France, Germany, Sweden, Japan, Canada, Austria, The Netherlands, Belgium, Great Britain, Finland, Australia, New Zealand, Italy, Spain, Greece, Chile, Korea, Israel, Hungary, Ireland, Czech Republic, Poland, Mexico, Turkey. Each bar has a grey Government / Compulsory segment (#BFBFBF) followed by a dark blue Voluntary segment (#00517A). Line chart titled China Consumer Confidence Proxy, subtitle Based on Average Z-Score* of Household Loans, Consumer Confidence Index, Passenger Car Sales, Air Passenger Traffic & Catering Consumption. Y-axis titled Consumer Confidence Proxy, China, unitless z-score, range -3 to 3 with labelled ticks at 3, 0 and -3, horizontal grid lines at each tick (grey). X-axis categories labelled 12/11, 6/12, 12/12, 6/13, 12/13, 6/14, 12/14, 6/15, 12/15, 6/16, 12/16, 6/17, 12/17, 6/18, 12/18 (semi-annual, roughly 100 monthly points). One series drawn as a navy line (#00517A, about 3 pt). Approximate values (no values printed): starts about -0.9 at 12/11, dips to about -1.2 in early 2012, about -0.6 near 12/12, peaks about +0.6 near 6/13 and 12/13, falls to about -0.6 near 6/14 and -0.9 near 12/14, rises to about +0.6 near 12/14 to 6/15, about -0.3 in 2015, peaks about +1.1 near 6/16 and 12/16, about +0.9 near 6/17, falls to about -0.4 near 12/17, about -0.7 near 6/18, then declines to about -1.7 at 9/18 and a trough of about -2.0 near 12/18, recovering to about -1.5 at the end. A green (#00B050) rectangular outline with square corners and about 2.5 pt stroke frames the period from 6/18 to the end of the series, spanning the full plot height from 3 to -3. No legend. Highlighted region is the green box.

### Slide 299

**Text**

China Urbanization = / Rising Rapidly…Room to Grow / Urban Population – % Total Population / 100% / % of Total Population / 50% / 0% / 1950 / 1967 / 1984 / 2001 / 2018 / USA / Japan / Korea / India / China / Source: CEIC, UN, Morgan Stanley Research / BOND / Internet Trends / 2019 / 298

**Layout**

Full-width navy title band across the top, about 12.5% of slide height, with the two-line title left-aligned at about 1.9% from the left edge. A single centred chart occupies the middle, with its chart title centred above the plot and a horizontal legend centred below the x-axis. A thin light grey rule sits near the bottom at about 93% height; the footer has the BOND Internet Trends 2019 mark at bottom left, a centred source line, the Hillhouse Capital logo at bottom right, and the page number 298 just right of the logo.

**Visuals**

Line chart titled 'Urban Population – % Total Population' (bold, dark slate #2A3137). Y-axis titled '% of Total Population', range 0% to 100%, gridlines at 0%, 50% and 100% in light grey; the y-axis label is rotated vertically. X-axis shows years 1950, 1967, 1984, 2001, 2018 (evenly spaced ticks, about 17-year steps). Five series, each a line with no markers, legend below in order USA (dark teal #00517A), Japan (yellow #FFC000), Korea (purple #7030A0), India (green #00B050), China (red #C00000, drawn thicker than the others). No values are printed; estimates: USA about 64% in 1950, about 70% in 1967, about 73% in 1975-1984, about 81% in 2018. Japan about 53% in 1950, about 70% in 1967, about 76% in 1984, about 79% in 2001, about 92% in 2018. Korea about 20% in 1950, about 32% in 1967, about 58% in 1984, about 78% in 2001, about 81% in 2018. India about 17% in 1950, about 21% in 1984, about 28% in 2001, about 33% in 2018. China about 11% in 1950, about 18% in 1960, about 20% in 1984, about 26% in 1998, about 48% in 2012, about 59% in 2018. A green rectangle (about #4CC38A, stroke about 0.5% of slide width, no fill) outlines the 2012 to 2018 span of the plot, from about 0% to 100% height, highlighting the right-hand end of the lines. The Hillhouse Capital logo: a red square with small white text at left, with the words 'Hillhouse' and 'Capital' in bold black to its right. The BOND mark at bottom left is a grey serif wordmark.

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. White slide background. Title band fill #00517A (dark teal blue) with white (#FFFFFF) Arial regular title text, two lines, font size about 4.4% of slide height. Chart title Arial Bold #2A3137, about 3.7% of slide height. Axis labels and source line in light grey #BFBFBF Arial, about 1.8% of slide height; source line about 1.3%. The footer carries a BOND / Internet Trends / 2019 mark at lower left, a centred grey source line, and a Hillhouse Capital logo with the page number 300 at lower right.

**Visuals**

One combined chart with the title China Current Account Balance in bold dark grey. Type: stacked column chart with a overlaid line series. Y axis: '% of GDP, China' with tick labels 12%, 8%, 4%, 0%, -4%, gridlines at each tick, range about -4% to 12%. X axis: years 2002 to 2018, labelled every two years, one column per half year. Series: Income & Transfer (green #00B050, stacked above zero in the positive region, and below zero in the negative region), Service Balance (yellow #FFC000, mostly negative after about 2010), Goods Balance (dark blue #00517A, the largest positive stack, peaking around 2007 at about 8.5% to 9%), and Current Account Balance (dark red line #C00000, peaking about 10% in 2007, falling to about 0.3% in 2018). Values are not printed on the slide, so readings are approximate: the current account line is about 2.4% in 2002, about 10% at the 2007 peak, about 1.2% in 2013, about 2.9% in 2014 and about 0.3% at the end in 2018. Legend below the plot, one row, with colour swatches in the order Income & Transfer, Service Balance, Goods Balance, Current Account Balance. No highlighted points. Logos: Hillhouse Capital logo (red square with white mark and black wordmark) at lower right; BOND wordmark in grey serif at lower left.

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. White background. Title band #00517A with white Arial-style sans-serif title text, regular weight, about 4.4% of slide height per line, with capitals about 3.1% high. Footer text: BOND and Internet Trends and 2019 in grey Georgia serif #C8C8C8, about 1.5%. Source line in light grey #BFBFBF Arial, about 1.3%. Page number 300 in grey #A6A6A6, about 1.5%. **Layout**

Two equal chart panels sit side by side below a full-width blue title band, separated by a thin vertical grey divider at the horizontal centre; the left panel spans about x 8 to 41 and the right about x 54 to 92. The title is left-aligned in the band at top-left with a margin of about 1.9% of the width, and the chart headings are centred above each panel. The footer has a thin grey rule across the full width at about y 93; the BOND mark and 'Internet Trends 2019' sit bottom-left, a centred two-line source note sits bottom-centre, and the Hillhouse Capital logo with page number 305 sits bottom-right. Three white-on-white date labels (2017-04, 2018-04, 2019-04) exist in the file at the bottom of each chart but are not visible.

**Visuals**

Two line charts. Left chart: title 'China Short-Form Video – Daily Time Spent'; single series, dark blue line (#00517A) with no legend; y-axis titled 'Daily Mobile Hours Spent' with labelled ticks 0, 300MM, 600MM (gridlines at 300MM and 600MM, light grey #D9D9D9); x-axis labelled 4/17, 4/18, 4/19 (one point per month, about 25 monthly points). No values are printed; about 56MM at the start (4/17), rising steadily to about 300MM near 4/18, and about 595MM at the last point (4/19), with a small dip near the late-2018 points. Right chart: title 'Leading Short-Form Video Platforms – DAUs'; three series with a legend below the plot reading Douyin (red line), Kuaishou (green line), Haokan (grey line); y-axis titled 'Daily Active Users' with ticks 0, 125MM, 250MM; x-axis labelled 4/17, 4/18, 4/19. No values are printed. Douyin (red #C00000) starts near 0, is about 60MM around late 2017, crosses Kuaishou at about 4/18 near 105MM, and ends about 237MM. Kuaishou (green #00B050) starts about 65MM, reaches about 105MM at 4/18, and ends about 210MM. Haokan (grey #A6A6A6) stays near 0 until about 2018, then rises to about 25MM at the end. No points are highlighted. Corner logos: a small BOND wordmark (grey serif) bottom-left, and the Hillhouse Capital logo (red square with tiny white wordmark, followed by the dark 'Hillhouse Capital' name in two lines) bottom-right. No photographs or icons.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF, covering the full slide. Clean corporate data slide with a flat white background and a single solid dark-teal title band across the top. Title text is white sans-serif regular at about 4.4% of slide height, with the second title line the same size. Chart headings are bold dark charcoal sans-serif at about 2.6% of slide height. Axis labels and tick labels are light grey sans-serif at about 1.8% of slide height. Legend and axis titles are dark charcoal or light grey. Footer source text is light grey sans-serif at about 1.3%; the BOND mark and 'Internet Trends 2019' use a grey Georgia serif at about 1.5%. Lines are thin (about 0.3% of slide height for series, about 0.1% for gridlines and divider), with square corners, no shadows and no gradients.

**Layout**

Full-width dark blue title band across the top, with a two-line left-aligned title starting about 1.9% from the left edge. Below it, a single stacked area chart fills the centre-left with its chart title centred above it, a vertical legend sits at the right (about 73% from the left), and a footer row holds the BOND wordmark, Internet Trends and 2019 at lower left, a centred source line, the Hillhouse Capital logo and page number 306 at lower right, separated from the content by a thin light-grey rule at about 93% of the height.

**Visuals**

One stacked area chart. Type: stacked area chart, linear value axis. Chart title: 'Average Smartphone Time Spent per MAU per Month' in bold dark grey. Y axis: label 'Hours per User per Month' (vertical, grey), ticks 0, 75 and 150 at the left of the plot, range 0 to 150. X axis: monthly categories Jan-15 to Apr-19, labelled every third month (Jan-15, Apr-15 and so on), labels rotated about 45 degrees in light grey, no units given. Series, bottom to top, with estimated values (about, no values printed): Communication & Social Networking dark blue #1E608B, about 30 to 45 hours from Jan-15 to Apr-19, rising slightly through 2018; Browser, Input Method, App Store light grey #C8C8C8, about 15 to 20 hours thick; Online Video green #66927D, about 10 to 15 hours thick; Games rose-brown #AC7A87, about 8 to 12 hours; News slate blue #6E79A3, about 5 to 8 hours; Shopping grey #A9B2BB, about 3 to 5 hours; Music pale blue #B6C6DD, about 3 to 6 hours; Reading near-white #E8E8E8, about 2 to 3 hours; Finance pale green #B5D5C5, about 1 to 3 hours; Other pale pink #D9B8BF, about 5 to 10 hours; Mobile Short Form Video crimson #E03169 on top, about 0 hours in Jan-15 rising to about 5 hours in early 2016, then about 10 to 20 hours from mid-2018, with peaks at about 25 hours around Jan-18 and Apr-19. Total stack about 80 hours in Jan-15, about 95 in 2016, about 105 in early 2018 and about 125 to 130 in Apr-19. Highlighted: the crimson Mobile Short Form Video band, the only saturated colour on the chart. Legend: vertical list at right, top to bottom in stack order (Mobile Short Form Video, Other, Finance, Reading, Music, Shopping, News, Games, Online Video, Browser Input Method App Store, Communication and Social Networking), each with a small square swatch and dark grey label. No data labels, no gridlines except a light grey top line at 150 and a grey baseline at 0.

**Design**

Background white. Title band solid #00517A with white title text. Chart title bold dark charcoal #2A3137. Legend and category labels dark charcoal #2A3137. Axis labels and tick labels light grey #BFBFBF. Footer text light grey: BOND wordmark #C8C8C8 serif, Internet Trends and 2019 #C8C8C8 Georgia serif, source line #BFBFBF Arial, page number #A6A6A6 Arial. Typefaces: title Arial (regular, sans-serif) at about 4.4% of slide height per line, with the word Incremental in Arial italic; chart title Arial bold at about 3.1%; legend and axis text Arial regular at about 1.8%; footer about 1.3 to 1.5%. Lines and shapes: thin grey top gridline at 150 and grey baseline at 0, a light grey footer rule; chart areas have no outlines and no shadows; no gradients, no rounded corners.

**Layout**

Below it, a centred bold subtitle 'Belle / TopSports' sits above two groups separated by a thin vertical grey divider at about 50% width: 'Store Managers' (left, two phone screenshots) and 'Store Associates' (right, two phone screenshots). Each screenshot has a centred two-line caption above it. A thin grey horizontal rule runs above the footer at about 93% height; the footer has the BOND logo at lower left, a centred grey source line, and the Hillhouse Capital logo with page number 311 at lower right.

**Visuals**

Four smartphone screenshots, each in a boxed frame with a dark charcoal (#333A40) border about 1% thick and square corners, shown upright and fully visible, not cropped. (1) Left, Store Managers, 'Real-time Sales by Category & SKU': a Chinese-language app screen titled 实时数据 with date 2019.05.16. Two donut charts: the upper donut has a centre label ¥74,999 and a caption 销售总额 and segments in blue, red, green and orange with leader lines to labels; the lower donut also shows ¥74,999 in its centre, with segments in purple, orange, teal and yellow and labels 儿童, 中性, 女子 and 男子. Four phone-screen screenshots, one per column, all portrait and shown whole (not cropped), each with a thick dark charcoal (#2A3137) border and a slight drop frame. **Layout**

A thin grey rule runs near 93% of height, with a source line centred beneath it, a BOND Internet Trends mark bottom-left, a Hillhouse Capital logo bottom-right and the page number 325 right of the logo.

**Visuals**

Eight photographs in a 4 by 2 grid, each boxed with a dark charcoal (#2A3137) rectangular frame of about 0.3% of slide height and no rounding. Row 1 left to right: (1) Freshippo/Hema: a grocery store storefront with a white cat-like logo and Chinese sign 盒马鲜生会员店 in white on dark, lit by overhead fluorescent light; shoppers queue at checkout counters with rope barriers, cool blue-white light, dominant colours dark navy, white and teal. (2) Sun Art: a supermarket aisle receding into the frame, shelves stocked with colourful packaged goods in pink, red, yellow and orange, a red overhead banner, white tiled floor; full frame, eye-level, bright even lighting. (3) Suning JV: a consumer electronics showroom with a large pink and purple backdrop bearing the Chinese text 七夕潮玩节 in white and pink neon, a red-and-white display table in front, dim purple-blue ambience. (4) Intime: a department store interior with a sign reading INTIME ONLINE in white capitals on a wooden ceiling strip, a woman and a child in a white jacket standing in the foreground, a wall-mounted screen and white-tiled floor, bright neutral lighting. Row 2 left to right: (5) Easy Home: a home-improvement showroom with a bright orange-red wall, a wall-mounted television, a white counter, a display with yellow flowers and a 618 promotional sticker, warm lighting. (6) Eleme & Koubei: an illustration on a near-black background with a white Starbucks siren logo, the word STARBUCKS in white capitals, the Chinese characters 我了么 in white at upper left, and a white line-art scooter delivery rider carrying a cup at bottom centre; no photographic depth, flat graphic style. (7) Tmall Store: a storefront with a large red top band bearing a black cat face and the Chinese text 天猫优品 in white, a glass door and shelves of clothing inside, red base strip along the bottom, bright even light. (8) LingShouTong: a convenience store interior with red-framed signage above, a glass display fridge, a counter and two staff in red uniforms, warm overhead light, dominant colours red, white and dark brown. None of the photographs are cropped beyond the frame, none are full-bleed, and none carry an overlay or tint.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. Clean corporate look on a white background. Title band fill #00517A (dark teal blue) with white title text in Arial regular, about 4.4% of slide height per line. Labels in Arial Bold, about 3.0% of slide height, colour #2A3137 (charcoal). Subtitles in Arial Italic, about 2.2% of slide height, colour #2A3137. Footer text: source line in Arial regular about 1.3% of height, colour #BFBFBF; BOND and Internet Trends in Georgia about 1.5%, colour #C8C8C8; page number in Arial about 1.5%, colour #A6A6A6. Photo frames charcoal #2A3137, square corners, no shadow. Hillhouse logo red #C8102E with dark text. No gradients.
